title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Democratic Senate candidates diverge on shielding ratepayers from data center costs.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Sunday morning, July 26, and yesterday's Democratic Senate primary debate gave voters their clearest look yet at who would protect electric bills as AI data centers ramp up demand.

That's the big story we're unpacking today. Candidates laid out different plans for regulating that electricity demand and deciding whether ratepayers or the companies themselves cover new transmission lines.

Exactly. Some want utilities or the tech firms to shoulder the upgrades. Others are open to spreading costs across all customers. Primary voters now have real differences to weigh on something that hits monthly bills.
Why does this matter so much right now? We've seen data centers popping up across the state, pulling hundreds of megawatts and millions of gallons of water. How did we get here so fast?

It's the AI boom. Hyperscale campuses need reliable power around the clock, and Michigan's location, water resources, and existing grid make it attractive. But that growth is colliding with local concerns over rates, noise, and farmland.
So when candidates talk about protecting ratepayers, what are the concrete options on the table?

From what we heard yesterday, some would push for special contracts where the data center operator or utility pays for any new lines or substations upfront. Others would allow those costs into the general rate base, meaning everyone sees a small bump.
And that difference could show up on my bill how?
A few dollars here and there for transmission, plus whatever the utility needs for new generation or upgrades. We've already seen added charges tied to earlier projects in some territories.

Indiana Michigan Power just pledged yesterday that residential customers in their southwest Michigan service area won't foot the bill for new data center lines. How does that fit into the bigger picture?

It's a direct response to the same pressure the candidates are feeling. The utility is trying to get ahead of rate-case fights by promising to shield households. Consumer groups and local officials will be watching to see if it holds when the numbers come in.
Meanwhile DTE's latest preview shows data-center growth as a key earnings driver. Does that mean higher profits for the company but potentially higher costs for customers?
That's the tension. More demand can boost utility revenue, but it also means more infrastructure that often gets recovered through rates. Michigan ratepayers have seen similar charges before.
So the Senate candidates are essentially debating who controls that cost recovery. What happens next in the primary?

Voters in August will pick the nominee, and this issue is now one of the clearest dividing lines. Whoever wins will carry it into the general election against the backdrop of more townships weighing their own rules.
Speaking of local pushback, several places moved this week. Garfield Township froze new data centers for at least a year after a sloppy application. What does that pause actually buy them?

Time to write proper zoning and siting rules before any big project locks in. Residents near the site were worried about power lines, water use, and property values. The board wants to get ahead of it.
Calhoun County commissioners are also debating a year-long halt over jobs versus power strain. How common are these moratoria becoming?

We're seeing them pop up in Delta County, Garfield, and now potentially Calhoun. Rural areas especially are hitting pause to study noise, water, and grid impacts before approving anything that could draw hundreds of megawatts.
Augusta Township is nearing a vote on rules for an Oracle-scale project that would pull from the same DTE territory as Saline. What's at stake there?
Zoning details and tax terms. A yes vote adds another large load on the grid and determines how much revenue the township actually keeps versus what ratepayers might absorb.
Saline Township flipped and restored Oracle's shot at a big tax break after earlier limits. That came after company lobbying. How do residents feel about trading tax revenue for jobs?

It's the classic trade-off. Supporters say the facility brings construction and operations work. Critics point to lost property-tax income for years on a multibillion-dollar project and the heavy power and water draw.
Over in Cass County, Dowagiac residents are reporting ongoing noise from an operating center's cooling systems. They're even talking legal options. Is that becoming more common?
It's one of the first places where the hum is already disrupting sleep. A potential class-action mention shows how quality-of-life issues can turn into real disputes once facilities are running.
And MLive just launched a map tracking every active fight by township and county. That sounds useful for listeners.
It shows proposals, hearings, moratoria, megawatts demanded, and tax deals in real time. You can see how your area compares to battles elsewhere.
So pulling it together, the Senate debate is the statewide frame, but the real action is still local with these pauses and rate fights. What should listeners watch this week?
Keep an eye on any rate-case filings from the utilities and how the candidates respond. Also watch whether more counties follow Delta and Garfield with their own one-year holds.
On deck, are there any public meetings listeners can actually attend tonight or tomorrow?
Nothing major scheduled that we're tracking right now. Check the Michigan Data Center Tracker for any last-minute additions.
Fair enough. Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.
